label: Cayley-Klein Geometries
notes: This chapter, printed pages 375 through 398, builds every classical geometry from one projective recipe: fix an absolute conic, then read distance and angle from cross-ratios formed with that conic. Emphasize that metric language is derived, not assumed, and that the conic's type decides which geometry we obtain.

label: The Absolute Conic
notes: Introduce the fundamental conic, the absolute, as the single piece of fixed data. A line meets it in two reference points and a pencil sees two reference tangents. Stress that all measuring uses only these projective intersections, so the construction is invariant under the projectivities that preserve the absolute.

label: Distance by Cross-Ratio
notes: State the core distance formula. The joining line of two points meets the absolute in X and Y, and half the constant times the logarithm of the cross-ratio gives the distance. Walk through why multiplicativity of cross-ratio becomes additivity of distance once a logarithm is applied.

label: Why the Logarithm Works
notes: This is the proof scaffold. Three cross-ratio identities give zero distance for coincident points, antisymmetry under swapping, and additivity along a line. Together they prove the logarithm of the cross-ratio is a genuine oriented scale before any specific model or geometry is named.

label: Three Behaviors on One Line
notes: On a fixed line the two absolute points fall into three cases. Real distinct points give a hyperbolic interval with an infinitely far boundary; complex conjugate points give a bounded elliptic scale; a coincident pair gives the parabolic limit requiring a chosen unit. One formula, three root types.

label: Angle as the Dual Measurement
notes: Angle is the dual of distance. From a point's pencil take the two tangents to the absolute, then measure the cross-ratio of two lines against those tangents. Show that for the circular points this reproduces Laguerre's Euclidean angle formula, confirming angle is just dual Cayley-Klein measurement.

label: Euclidean: I and J Revisited
notes: Euclidean geometry is not outside the scheme. Its absolute is the degenerate doubly counted line at infinity carrying the imaginary circular points I and J. Distance becomes parabolic and needs a calibrated unit, while angle is elliptic, measured against I and J exactly as Laguerre prescribed.

label: A Real Planar Absolute
notes: Take the unit circle as absolute. One plane now shows every behavior: secant lines give real hyperbolic intervals, missing lines give elliptic measurement, tangents give the parabolic boundary, and separated points force an imaginary part. Constant-distance curves inside the Klein disk are genuine projective conics.

label: Hyperbolic and Elliptic Models
notes: Contrast the two nondegenerate planes. A real absolute conic gives the hyperbolic Klein disk, whose boundary sits at infinite real distance. An imaginary conic leaves no real boundary and gives the elliptic plane, modeled by a sphere with antipodal points identified. Both come from the same formula.

label: The Seven-Type Census
notes: Classification reduces to the real projective equivalence class of the conic pair. Seven types span nondegenerate, singly degenerate, and doubly degenerate cases. Read the table: each row fixes the absolute object and the resulting distance and angle behavior, recovering elliptic, hyperbolic, Euclidean, Minkowski, and Galilean planes.

label: The Distance-Angle Grid
notes: Summarize with the coarser grid. Distance and angle are each independently hyperbolic, elliptic, or parabolic, giving a three by three menu of geometries. Point out the diagonal classical cases and the off-diagonal mixed planes like Minkowski and Galilean, all selected purely by the absolute conic.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: Close by collecting the unifying message. The absolute conic supplies the reference elements; cross-ratio multiplicativity becomes distance additivity through the logarithm; hyperbolic, elliptic, and parabolic are root-type cases, not separate theories. Euclidean is type V, hyperbolic lives inside type II, elliptic is type I.
